query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a stepwise sequence of disparate coherent nano-precipitates through a multistage thermo-mechanical processing can improve the mechanical performance of refractory high-entropy alloys while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys with a dual-phase structure
generation.intervention: Multistage thermo-mechanical processing to generate a stepwise sequence of disparate coherent nano-precipitates
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nano-precipitates with distinct nanoscale structures
generation.mechanism: Precipitation hardening and progressive multistage strain hardening
generation.predicted_outcome: Ultrahigh yield strength and tensile ductility at both ambient and elevated temperatures
generation.uncertainty: The effectiveness of this approach in maintaining thermal and irradiation stability over extended periods

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical performance of refractory high-entropy alloys with and without the stepwise sequence of disparate coherent nano-precipitates under high-temperature and irradiation-exposed conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of the stepwise sequence of disparate coherent nano-precipitates does not result in improved mechanical performance, the hypothesis is falsified

A emerging paradigm for the development of metallic materials has been the notion of multiple-principal-element alloys, often termed as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or compositionally complex alloys (CCAs), which has presented promising pathways for seeking improved alloys within a previously unexplored compositional/phase space. Numerous mechanistic phenomena have been studied to induce significant strengthening and toughening in these alloy systems, which serve to improve their strength-ductility synergy; these include high lattice friction, interstitial solid solution, grain refinement and gradients in grain size, in situ phase transformation, and nano-precipitation. Of note here is the approach of incorporating nano-precipitates that have a positive influence on both strength and ductility. In this work, we utilize the immense compositional space of multiple-principal-element alloys to develop a promising tungsten-based refractory HEA with a dual-phase structure. We show that by exploiting the high melting-temperature alloy characteristics of this HEA and modulating its composition, it is possible to generate a stepwise sequence of disparate coherent nano-precipitates over different phase-transition temperature ranges to achieve a combination of ultra-high strength and tensile ductility at both ambient and elevated temperatures (800 °C). Specifically, by departing from the traditional W-Fe-Ni compositions of tungsten heavy alloys, we design a (W1.5Ni2.25Fe)95Ta5 (at.%) refractory HEA with a stepwise and independently controllable dual coherent precipitation structure. With this strategy, we first control the Ni/Fe ratio to be between 2 and 4 to avoid the formation of the topologically close-packed μ phase at phase boundaries,. ajority of an aeroengine turbine component’s service life is spent at intermediate temperatures. As a result, in addition to being able to withstand short bursts at peak operating temperatures, it is critical that the performance of a high temperature alloy does not degrade during extended exposures at the lower temperature experienced during cruise. Since an alloy’s properties are intrinsically linked to its microstructural condition, maintaining performance under these operating conditions requires a high level of microstructural stability. Therefore, characterising the microstructural stability of an alloy both at peak and average service temperatures is crucial to evaluating its suitability for high temperature service.
The recent development of refractory metal high-entropy superalloys (RSA), based on the AlMoNbTaTiZr system, has attracted significant attention as they have the potential for use in structural applications at temperatures higher than currently accessible [,]. Initial results have shown that these RSA have certain advantages over current Ni-based superalloys, including lower densities and higher compressive strengths []. of the phases within the microstructures is also different. The matrix phase of the Ni-based superalloy is the more ductile disordered phase, whilst in RSA the matrix is the ordered phase. As such, despite the attractive high temperature strengths, the ordered matrix phase and the presence of Al-Zr intermetallics leads to very limited room temperature ductility and the implications that this has for toughness is a key concern for potential applications []. Significant efforts have already been made to invert the microstructure of RSA and suppress the formation of the Al-Zr-rich grain boundary phase, details of these studies can be found elsewhere [,,,].
Despite its critical importance to potential applications, little is known about the thermal stability of RSA microstructures. Relatively few studies have considered thermal exposures at temperatures below the B2 solvus and, even then, the reported durations are relatively short [,,,,,,,,].
